openingProblem.problem: In January 1950 the US did not treat Korea as vital. By 1953 it had fought a three-year war there, against China as well as North Korea, and the war had ended where it began, at the 38th parallel. Why did a war that changed no borders change the whole Cold War?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: what was the Korean War's most important consequence?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Origins: a divided peninsula, 1945–1950
chunks.body:
Korea was divided by the Cold War before it was fought over. During the Second World War the United States and the Soviet Union agreed to divide the peninsula temporarily at the **38th parallel** to oversee the surrender and removal of Japanese forces. Neither superpower would then let its Korean ally be absorbed by the other. The Soviets backed the Communist leader **Kim Il Sung** in the North, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea; the Americans backed **Syngman Rhee** in the South, the Republic of Korea.

Yet the US did not treat Korea as vital. It left Korea out of the core of its defensive strategy in East Asia, and American forces withdrew from the South in the late 1940s. Kim drew his conclusion: the US, he assumed, did not consider South Korea worth fighting for. On **25 June 1950** the North Korean army launched a coordinated attack across the 38th parallel, aiming to conquer the South and unify Korea under Communist rule.

Who was responsible? Kim launched the attack, but Tony Judt calls Stalin's support for it "his most serious miscalculation of all". The context mattered too. The Communist victory in China in 1949 and the first Soviet atomic test had shaken Washington, and the National Security Council had just completed **NSC-68**, which described a Soviet Union bent on world domination and called for a massive military build-up.

Washington read the invasion through that lens. Truman, concerned that the Soviet Union and Communist China might have encouraged the attack, committed American air, naval and ground forces to a United Nations force to defend the South, under General **Douglas MacArthur**. Americans and West Europeans, Judt writes, drew the "erroneous" conclusion that Korea was a diversion or a prelude, and that Germany would be next.

This mattered because a local war of unification was interpreted as a test of containment, which meant that a peninsula the US had not considered vital became a battleground of the global Cold War.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The superpowers' division of Korea created two rival regimes.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The war was also a Korean civil war over unification.

argumentsThatWork.claim: American signals of disengagement encouraged Kim to attack.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Kim's aim was unification, which both Korean regimes wanted.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Stalin's support was a miscalculation that globalised the conflict.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The West misread the invasion as a prelude to an attack on Europe.

howItGetsAsked: Examine the causes and consequences of the Korean War (1950–1953).
Compare and contrast the roles of the United States and China in the Korean War between 1950 and 1953.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Korean War was caused by the division of Korea combined with Kim's belief that the US would not defend the South.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The superpowers had divided Korea at the 38th parallel, and after US forces withdrew in the late 1940s Kim attacked on 25 June 1950.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that a war for unification began, but because Washington believed the USSR and China were behind it, it became a Cold War conflict.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Judt argues that Stalin's support for the invasion was his 'most serious miscalculation', so the Soviet role turned a local war into a global crisis.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The war's causes were therefore Korean in origin but Cold War in their consequences.

chunks.title: War of movement, June–December 1950
chunks.body:
The first months were a war of rapid movement up and down the peninsula. The North Korean attack drove the defenders back to a narrow perimeter around the port of **Pusan** in the far south. Once the front stabilised there, MacArthur struck. In September 1950 he made a surprise amphibious landing at **Inchon**, far behind North Korean lines, and the North Koreans retreated behind the 38th parallel.

The UN had now achieved its original aim: the South was saved. But in October the United Nations, urged by the United States, approved sending UN forces across the 38th parallel to unify Korea under a non-Communist government. Containment had become rollback. The Chinese government issued warnings, but UN forces advanced towards the **Yalu River**, Korea's border with Manchuria. MacArthur discounted the first Chinese attacks in late October and ordered an offensive to reach the Yalu.

In late November China attacked in full strength. The UN forces were driven back in disarray south of the 38th parallel, and Communist forces seized the South Korean capital, Seoul. American and Chinese soldiers were now fighting each other directly.

China had its own reasons to fight. At the start of the war the US had sent its Seventh Fleet into the Taiwan Strait to stop the conflict spreading south, which also blocked a Communist invasion of Taiwan. The Chinese moved the troops they had gathered for that invasion to the Korean front. An American army approaching China's border, from a power that protected its civil-war enemy on Taiwan, looked like a direct threat.

This mattered because the decision to cross the 38th parallel turned a successful defence into a wider war, which meant that the US was now fighting the People's Republic of China.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Inchon reversed the war and saved the South.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The North had almost conquered the peninsula first.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Crossing the 38th parallel turned containment into rollback.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The UN, not only the US, approved it.

argumentsThatWork.claim: China intervened when UN forces approached its border.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: China had issued warnings that MacArthur discounted.

howItGetsAsked: To what extent was the decision to cross the 38th parallel the main reason for Chinese intervention in the Korean War in 1950?

useItInAnEssay.claim: The decision to cross the 38th parallel was the main reason for Chinese intervention, because it brought an American-led army to China's border.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In October 1950 the UN, urged by the US, approved crossing the parallel to unify Korea, and despite Chinese warnings UN forces advanced towards the Yalu.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that China faced a hostile army on the border of Manchuria, so in late November it attacked in full strength and retook Seoul.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, China already saw the US as a threat, since the Seventh Fleet had blocked its planned invasion of Taiwan in June 1950.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Crossing the parallel was therefore the trigger, while the wider US threat to China explains why the warning was serious.

chunks.title: Limited war and stalemate, 1951–1953
chunks.body:
In early 1951 the Chinese offensive lost momentum. UN forces, revived under General Matthew Ridgway, retook Seoul and pushed back to the 38th parallel. From July 1951 the front barely moved, and the war became a **stalemate**. The Truman administration abandoned the aim of reuniting Korea and settled for limited goals, to avoid a third world war involving China and the Soviet Union.

Not everyone accepted limits. General MacArthur publicly challenged the administration's conduct of the war. Truman concluded that MacArthur was "unable to give his wholehearted support to the policies of the United States Government" and relieved him of his command in April 1951. The principle that civilian leaders, not generals, decided how far a war would go was reaffirmed.

The nuclear question hung over the war. Truman deployed B-29 bombers to signal American resolve. In 1953 President Eisenhower considered using the threat of nuclear weapons to push the ceasefire talks forward, but rejected the idea. Eisenhower had promised during his election campaign to go to Korea, and he did so on 2 December 1952. He concluded that "we could not stand forever on a static front and continue to accept casualties without any visible results." He sought an end through a combination of diplomacy and "military muscle-flexing".

The **armistice** was signed on **27 July 1953**. It ended organised combat but left Korea divided much as it had been since 1945, near the 38th parallel. In 1953 the United States signed a mutual security treaty with South Korea to protect it from the North.

This mattered because both sides accepted a war with limited aims, which meant that the Cold War's first major hot war ended in a draw rather than escalating into a world war.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Truman chose limited war to avoid a world war.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: MacArthur and others wanted to widen the war.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Civilian control was reaffirmed by MacArthur's dismissal.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The dismissal was politically costly for Truman.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Nuclear weapons were threatened but not used.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The threat may have helped bring the armistice.

Discuss the view that the Korean War was a success for the United States with reference to the period 1950 to 1953.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Korean War remained limited mainly because Truman decided that a wider war with China and the USSR was too dangerous.
useItInAnEssay.prove: From July 1951 the front was stable, and the administration abandoned reunification for limited goals to avoid a third world war.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that when MacArthur publicly challenged this policy, Truman relieved him in April 1951, so civilian control kept the war limited.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, nuclear threats were part of the war: Truman deployed B-29s, and Eisenhower considered nuclear coercion in 1953 before rejecting it.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The war therefore stayed limited by political choice, though the danger of escalation never disappeared.

chunks.title: Consequences: the Cold War militarised and globalised
chunks.body:
The Korean War transformed the Cold War far beyond Korea.

**In the United States**, it turned NSC-68 into policy. Judt argues that NSC-68's budget increases "would almost certainly not have been approved but for the Korean attack". The US defence budget rose from $15.5 billion in August 1950 to $70 billion by December 1951. By 1952–53 defence consumed 17.8 per cent of American GNP, against 4.7 per cent in 1949.

**In Europe**, the war was read as a warning. Believing that Germany might be next, the United States increased its troop commitments, and every NATO member raised its defence spending to a post-war peak in 1951–53. NATO became, in Judt's words, "unambiguously, an alliance", with Eisenhower as Supreme Allied Commander and a target, set at Lisbon in February 1952, of ninety-six new divisions. The only way to meet it was to rearm the West Germans, which the US Secretary of State Dean Acheson formally proposed in September 1950. The war also changed Europe's economy: the Marshall Plan was turned into a programme of military aid, prices rose (by 40 per cent in France in two years), and, Judt writes, "it was Korea, not Schuman, that sent the West German industrial machine into high gear".

**In Asia**, the war fixed the lines of the Cold War. The US committed itself to defending Taiwan and to isolating the People's Republic, imposing an embargo that lasted for two decades; any chance of accommodation between Washington and Beijing ended. It signed a security treaty with South Korea. And it accelerated the restoration of Japan: the peace treaty and a US-Japanese Security Treaty were signed on 8 September 1951, making Japan part of America's containment system.

There were consequences for Moscow too. Stalin, informed of the American build-up, wrongly assumed the US had aggressive designs on Eastern Europe, and dropped a planned attack on Yugoslavia in the face of Western rearmament. In the Eisenhower Library's assessment, the war prevented North Korea from imposing Communist rule on the South and showed that the US would fight aggression.

This mattered because a war on the edge of Asia militarised the Cold War everywhere, which meant that after 1953 both blocs faced each other with permanent, heavily armed alliances.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was the decision to cross the 38th parallel the main reason for Chinese intervention in the Korean War in 1950?
essayQuestions.namedFactor: the decision to cross the 38th parallel

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: Whether the crossing outweighed China's wider fear of the US

modelPlan.thesis: The decision to cross the 38th parallel was the main reason, because it brought an American-led army to China's border despite Chinese warnings; but China already saw the US as a threat after the Seventh Fleet blocked its invasion of Taiwan.

arguments.claim: Crossing the parallel and the advance to the Yalu (named factor first).
Chinese warnings ignored.
The Seventh Fleet and Taiwan.
US hostility to the PRC since 1949.

modelPlan.counter: The Chinese troops gathered for Taiwan were moved to the Korean front from mid-1950, before the parallel was crossed.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Would China have intervened if the UN had stopped at the 38th parallel? Probably not in November 1950, so the crossing was decisive.

segments.text: The decision to cross the 38th parallel was the main reason for Chinese intervention.
In October 1950 the UN, urged by the US, approved crossing to unify Korea, and despite Chinese warnings UN forces advanced towards the Yalu.
This meant that China faced a hostile army on its border, so in late November it attacked in full strength.
However, China already saw the US as a threat, since the Seventh Fleet had entered the Taiwan Strait in June 1950 and blocked its plans for Taiwan.
Crossing the parallel was therefore the decisive trigger of an intervention that wider hostility had made likely.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “The Korean War was a success for the United States.” Discuss with reference to the period 1950 to 1953.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The claim: a success for the US
decodeKey.judgement: By what criterion: saving the South, or reunifying Korea?

modelPlan.thesis: The war was a success by the original aim of saving South Korea, but a failure by the later aim of reunifying Korea, and it brought the US into a costly war with China that fixed Cold War hostility in Asia.

arguments.claim: For: the South survived; aggression was resisted.
For: NATO and the build-up strengthened the West.
Against: rollback failed and China intervened.
Against: stalemate and division at the original line.

modelPlan.counter: The Eisenhower Library's assessment stresses success in showing US willingness to combat aggression.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: By containment, success; by rollback, failure.

segments.text: The Korean War was a success for the US in containing Communism, but not in reunifying Korea.
Inchon saved the South in September 1950, but the advance across the 38th parallel brought China in, and the armistice of 27 July 1953 left Korea divided where it began.
This meant that the US achieved its original aim but failed in the wider aim it adopted in October 1950.
However, the war also brought a huge Western build-up and turned NATO into a real alliance, which strengthened the US globally.
The claim is therefore valid by the criterion of containment, but not by that of rollback.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the causes and consequences of the Korean War (1950–1953).

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The war was caused by Korea's division and Kim's belief that the US would not defend the South, with Stalin's support; its main consequence was the militarisation of the Cold War far beyond Korea.

arguments.claim: Cause: division and US disengagement.
Cause: Stalin's support for the invasion.
Consequence: the NSC-68 build-up.
Consequence: NATO, German rearmament and Asian alignments.

modelPlan.counter: The war changed no borders in Korea itself.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The militarisation of containment and NATO.

segments.text: The Korean War was caused by the division of Korea and Kim's belief that the US would not defend the South.
After US forces withdrew in the late 1940s, Kim attacked on 25 June 1950 with Stalin's support, which Judt calls 'his most serious miscalculation of all'.
This meant that the West read the attack as a global threat, so NSC-68 became policy and US defence spending rose from $15.5 billion to $70 billion.
However, in Korea itself the war ended where it began, near the 38th parallel.
Its most significant consequence was therefore the militarisation of the Cold War, especially in Europe.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the reasons why the Korean War remained a limited war between 1950 and 1953.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh the reasons, then judge

modelPlan.thesis: The war stayed limited mainly because Truman decided that a wider war with China and the USSR was too dangerous, enforcing that choice by relieving MacArthur; nuclear restraint under Eisenhower confirmed it.

arguments.claim: Truman's choice of limited goals.
Civilian control: MacArthur relieved.
Nuclear restraint.
Stalemate pushed both sides to an armistice.

modelPlan.counter: The nuclear threat itself may have helped end the war.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason mattered most? Truman's political decision, without which MacArthur's strategy might have widened the war.

segments.text: The war stayed limited mainly because Truman chose limited aims to avoid a third world war.
From July 1951 the administration abandoned reunification, and when MacArthur publicly challenged this, Truman relieved him in April 1951.
This meant that the war's aims were set by civilians who feared escalation, so the conflict stayed confined to Korea.
However, nuclear weapons were never far away: B-29s were deployed, and Eisenhower considered nuclear coercion in 1953 before rejecting it.
Political restraint was therefore the decisive reason, confirmed by the rejection of nuclear escalation.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the roles of the United States and China in the Korean War between 1950 and 1953.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The roles of the US and China

modelPlan.thesis: Both entered the war to defend an allied Korean state and both accepted a limited outcome, but the US entered to contain aggression and briefly sought rollback, while China entered to defend its border, and the war isolated China while strengthening the US globally.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both defended an allied Korean state.
Similarity: both accepted stalemate and armistice.
Difference: containment and rollback against defence of the border.
Difference: outcomes for each power.

modelPlan.counter: Both acted partly from fear of the other, which narrows the difference.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? The outcome: the US gained allies and strength, China isolation.

segments.text: The US and China both fought to defend an allied Korean state, but for different reasons and with different results.
The US entered in June 1950 to resist aggression it believed was Soviet-backed, whereas China attacked in November 1950 when UN forces approached its border.
This meant that the US briefly tried to unify Korea, while China fought to push a hostile army back from the Yalu.
However, both accepted limited aims after 1951 and signed the armistice in 1953.
The decisive difference was therefore the outcome: the war strengthened the US globally but isolated China for two decades.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the impact of the Korean War on the Cold War in Europe between 1950 and 1953.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: How a war in Asia changed Europe

modelPlan.thesis: The Korean War militarised the Cold War in Europe: it turned NATO into a real alliance, led to plans for West German rearmament, transformed the Marshall Plan into military aid and boosted West German industry.

arguments.claim: Fear that Germany would be next.
NATO as an alliance; Lisbon targets.
West German rearmament and industry.
Costs: prices and military aid.

modelPlan.counter: The risk of a European war was, Judt argues, greatly exaggerated.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: How did the parts connect? Fear of a European Korea led to NATO targets that only German rearmament could meet.

segments.text: The Korean War militarised the Cold War in Europe, although no fighting took place there.
Fearing that Germany would be next, NATO members raised defence spending to post-war peaks, and at Lisbon in February 1952 set a target of ninety-six new divisions.
This meant that the West needed more troops than it had, so Acheson proposed West German rearmament in September 1950.
However, Judt argues that the risk of a European war was greatly exaggerated, so the response rested on a misreading of Soviet intentions.
Korea's impact on Europe was therefore profound but based on a misunderstanding, which Stalin mirrored by misreading the American build-up.
